structure.overview: This case concerns an appeal regarding the reasonableness of delay between conviction and sentencing under section 11(b) of the Charter. The appellant challenges the sentencing delay, advocating for a five-month presumptive ceiling, while the Crown supports a flexible approach. The Supreme Court adopts the Crown's flexible 'markedly longer' test for assessing sentencing delay, finds the delay unreasonable, and upholds the Court of Appeal's reduction of the sentence as the appropriate remedy.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Section heading introducing the background of the case.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court in Jordan set presumptive ceilings of 18 months for provincial and 30 months for superior court trials to address delay under s. 11(b).

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The appeal concerns assessing delay reasonableness between conviction and sentencing, with appellant favoring a five-month ceiling and Crown a flexible approach.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court adopts the Crown's flexible standard, noting sentencing requires evidence and submissions after guilt is found.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Reasonableness of sentencing delay depends on factors like duration, complexity, parties' conduct, and local case timing.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: If s. 11(b) breach occurs post-verdict, remedy is usually sentence reduction, with stays rare; s. 24(1) allows discretion.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Section heading introducing decisions below.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: On Dec 13, 2021, defence requested adjournment for transcript; sentencing submissions scheduled for Feb 25, 2022.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: On Feb 25, 2022, sentencing submissions began but Crown couldn't finish due to technical issues; hearing continued April 5.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: On April 5, 2022, another judge adjourned due to trial judge unavailability; rescheduled for April 19, 2022.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: On May 24, 2022, trial judge questioned counsel; written responses agreed; next date set for July 12, 2022.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: On July 12, 2022, another judge adjourned due to trial judge emergency; rescheduled to Sept 16, 2022.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: On Sept 16, 2022, trial judge not ready to sentence, sought immigration info; continuation set for Oct 20, 2022.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: On Oct 20, 2022, defence filed stay application for unreasonable sentencing delay; appellant waived delay for Crown response.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: On Dec 16, 2022, trial judge dismissed s. 11(b) application and sentenced appellant to conditional sentence and probation.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Section heading introducing Ontario Court of Justice decision by Redgate J.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Trial judge found 378-day sentencing delay, deducted 74 days for defence, 80 for unavailability, 69 for complexity, 39 for submissions delay.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Trial judge concluded net delay was 116 days, under five-month ceiling, and dismissed s. 11(b) application.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Section heading introducing issues before the Court of Appeal.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Court of Appeal found net delay 225 days, exceeding five-month ceiling, thus infringing s. 11(b).

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Court of Appeal reduced sentence to 20 months due to delay, rejected conditional discharge, and considered immigration consequences.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Section heading introducing analysis.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Section heading introducing Jordan presumptive ceilings for trial delay.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Jordan replaced Morin framework with presumptive ceilings to combat delay culture and protect accused and public interests.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Jordan set 18- and 30-month ceilings for provincial and superior courts, deducting defence delays; exceeding ceiling shifts burden to Crown.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Below ceiling, defence must show meaningful steps and marked delay; assessment is contextual, not mathematical.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Jordan ceilings apply only to charge-to-trial end, not post-verdict delay, which was not addressed by Jordan majority.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Ontario Court of Appeal in Charley applied s. 11(b) to sentencing delay, creating a separate five-month ceiling for post-verdict delay.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Charley rejected flexible approach, holding presumptive ceilings essential to avoid uncertainty and complacency in sentencing delay.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: K.G.K. declined to extend Jordan ceilings to verdict deliberation, adopting a standard of marked longer delay due to judicial integrity presumption.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Heading introducing the topic of variability in sentencing proceedings and their unsuitability for presumptive ceilings.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court declines to follow Charley or impose presumptive ceilings for post-verdict sentencing delay due to lack of evidentiary foundation and sentencing variability.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Heading introducing the rationale for presumptive ceilings not applying to post-verdict sentencing delay.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court lists legitimate reasons for extended sentencing time, emphasizing the need for informed and proportionate sentences.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Sentencing may take longer due to systemic and background factors affecting Indigenous and racialized offenders, requiring specialized assessments.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Criminal Code mandates an individualized sentencing process with provisions allowing evidence and submissions to ensure fairness and completeness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Sentencing judges must control proceedings by setting clear positions, timelines, and encouraging collaboration to avoid unnecessary delay.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Sentencing proceedings vary greatly in length and complexity depending on case specifics, requiring flexible timing.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Heading introducing the test for assessing reasonableness of post-verdict sentencing delay as the 'markedly longer' test.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court explains Jordan's presumptive ceilings address trial delay complacency, not sentencing delay, emphasizing systemic change needs.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court notes prior refusals to extend Jordan ceilings to other proceedings without evidence of systemic delay problems.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court rejects the appellant's argument of complacency in sentencing delay due to lack of evidentiary record showing systemic problems.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court declines to follow Charley, emphasizing the need for evidence of systemic problems before imposing presumptive ceilings on sentencing.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Heading introducing the consistency and simplicity of the 'markedly longer' test with s. 11(b) jurisprudence.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Different provinces use varied tests for post-verdict sentencing delay, including 'markedly longer', MacDougall, and flexible approaches.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Crown supports the 'markedly longer' test for clarity; the appellant opposes it as replicating Morin's unpredictability and burdening defence.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court endorses the 'markedly longer' test as consistent, clear, and suitable for sentencing's individualized nature and interests balance.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Heading introducing considerations informing whether post-verdict delay was markedly longer than reasonably necessary.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Applying the 'markedly longer' test uniformly to sentencing avoids artificial distinctions and respects judicial integrity presumption.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The 'markedly longer' standard fits the post-guilt balance where offender's s.11(b) interests are attenuated and society's interest in prompt sentencing is heightened.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Heading introducing that remedies for unreasonable post-verdict sentencing delay are discretionary.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The 'markedly longer' standard is objective and normative, assessing delay in an ideal justice system, not current resource-limited realities.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The standard requires contextual comparison of actual sentencing time to reasonable time considering all circumstances.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Factors from K.G.K. for verdict deliberation time can guide assessing whether sentencing delay was markedly longer than reasonable.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Extreme post-verdict delay alone may breach s.11(b), but usually the analysis starts with length, which rarely alone meets the threshold.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Case complexity is key in assessing delay, including evidence, co-accused, legal issues, reports, and associated proceedings.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Reasons for specific delay periods, including medical emergencies or report delays, are relevant to the markedly longer analysis.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Parties' conduct and timing of legal issues affect whether delay was markedly longer than reasonable.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Comparing elapsed time to typical case durations in local contexts helps assess reasonableness, though systemic issues may limit this.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The markedly longer standard encourages timely sentencing without excusing delays caused by systemic underfunding or deficiencies.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states local circumstances matter but cannot justify systemic under-resourcing causing unreasonable post-verdict delay in sentencing.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Heading introducing the qualitative difference in balancing interests under section 11(b) during post-verdict sentencing phase.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court explains Rahey's stay remedy applies pre-conviction but not post-verdict, where the remedial question differs.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The appellant argues only a stay or absolute discharge can remedy post-verdict delay; the Crown argues for no automatic stay due to differing interests post-conviction.
idea_list: appellant: only stay or discharge remedy
Crown: no automatic stay, interests differ post-conviction

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court agrees with the Crown that stay is not automatic post-verdict; remedies must be discretionary and consider both offender and public interests.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Heading introducing section 24(1) of the Charter conferring broad remedial discretion.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: After conviction, the balance shifts from individual interests to society's interest in resolving criminal matters with a fit sentence.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The offender's s. 11(b) interests narrow after conviction, reflecting loss of presumption of innocence.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: A convicted offender's liberty interests differ from an untried accused; delay may prolong detention but is tied to adjudicated guilt.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Post-conviction delay causes stress and anxiety but differs qualitatively from pre-conviction uncertainty due to established guilt.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Fair-trial interests diminish post-verdict as evidentiary record is preserved and sentencing allows wide latitude for information.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Society's interest in proper criminal disposition grows post-conviction, focusing on appropriate sanctions as reflected in the Criminal Code.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court summarizes that post-verdict s. 11(b) interests are attenuated and societal interests heightened, making automatic stay unsuitable.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Heading introducing the application section of the decision.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states remedies must respond to Charter breaches post-verdict without undermining the lawful finding of guilt.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The usual remedy for unreasonable post-verdict delay is a reduced sentence to address harms caused by the delay.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Delay can be mitigating even without Charter breach, but reduction for unconstitutional delay is a distinct constitutional remedy.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Section 24(1) allows broad remedies; stay is rare and reserved for clear cases after considering all factors.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: A stay post-verdict stops sentencing but does not affect valid guilt finding; nullifying conviction would be unjustified.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court emphasizes wide remedial discretion under s. 24(1) allowing tailored remedies beyond formulaic approaches.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Heading introducing the conclusion section of the decision.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The trial judge's management of collateral immigration consequences was incremental and inefficient, causing unreasonable sentencing delay.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Various adjournments cumulatively contributed to delay exceeding reasonable time for sentencing.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Court of Appeal reduced the conditional sentence from 2 years less a day to 20 months as remedy for s. 11(b) violation due to delay.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Heading introducing the overview section of the decision.
